title: Tessellation of Shapes
subtitle: Why some shapes tile forever and some leave a gap.
objectives: Define a tessellation as a covering with no gaps and no overlaps
Identify the three regular polygons that tessellate on their own
Calculate the interior angle of a regular polygon and test it against 360°
Explain why some regular polygons cannot tessellate
Create a tessellating tile using the cut-and-slide method

cards.title: Every game map you've played is one of these
cards.text: Open a strategy game and the world is squares or hexagons. That's not decoration. It's the only way a map can go on forever without breaking.

cards.title: Two rules, no exceptions
cards.text: A tessellation is a pattern of shapes covering a flat surface. It has to obey exactly two rules.
points: **No gaps.** Not one bare patch anywhere.
**No overlaps.** Nothing sits on top of anything else.
**It could go on forever** if you had the room.

cards.title: Only three regular shapes work alone
cards.text: Triangle, square, hexagon. That's the complete list, and it has been for as long as flat surfaces have existed.

question.text: Which of these breaks the rules of a tessellation?
options: A pattern with a small gap between some tiles
A pattern of squares in a grid
question.explain: Any gap disqualifies it. So does any overlap. The shapes have to fit exactly.

cards.title: This is why tilesets exist
cards.text: A game world isn't drawn once. It's a small set of tiles repeated across a grid.
points: **Squares are the default.** Easy to store, easy to index.
**Hex grids** show up in strategy games — six neighbours, not eight.
**Minecraft is the 3D version.** Cubes tessellate space, not just a plane.

cards.title: The answer is always at one corner
cards.text: Pick any point where tiles meet. The angles around it must add to exactly 360° — a full turn. More and they overlap. Less and there's a gap.

cards.title: Fan the shapes around one point
cards.text: Tap through the shapes. Watch the gap close on three of them, and refuse to on the others.

cards.title: Finding the corner angle
cards.text: For a regular polygon with n sides, each interior angle is (n − 2) × 180 ÷ n.
points: **Then ask:** does it divide into 360 exactly?

question.text: What is the interior angle of a regular hexagon, in degrees? Digits only.

cards.title: Where the pentagon goes wrong
cards.text: A regular pentagon's corner is 108°. Three of them make 324°.
points: **That's 36° short** of a full turn.
**Four would be 432°** — now they overlap.
**There's no whole number** that lands on 360. So it can't.

cards.text: A regular octagon fails too — 135° each, and two make only 270°. That's why a tiled floor of stop signs always needs little squares in the gaps.

cards.title: The angle test, worked through
cards.text: The same calculation you just did, done out loud. Good to replay before the exam.

question.text: A shape's interior angle is 100°. Can it tessellate on its own?
question.explain: 360 ÷ 100 = 3.6. You'd fit three with 60° left over. The division has to come out exact.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: You've got the rule and the reason. Part 3 is where it stops being maths class and starts being art. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Nature picked one of the three
cards.text: Of the shapes that tile, hexagons keep showing up on their own — in hives, in rock formations, in engineering. There's a reason.

cards.title: Race cars are full of hexagons
cards.text: Look inside a Formula 1 floor or a crash structure and you'll find aluminium honeycomb.
points: **Hexagons tile with no wasted material.**
**Huge stiffness for almost no weight.**
**Carbon fibre weave** is a tessellation too — squares, on the diagonal.

cards.text: Bees use hexagons because that shape encloses the most space for the least wall. Less wax, more honey. Mathematicians only proved they were right in 1999.

cards.title: A honeycomb, built to the rule
cards.alt: A bee honeycomb, showing hexagonal cells packed together with no gaps
cards.credit: Pearson Scott Foresman · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
cards.text: Hexagons, no gaps, no wasted wall. Bees got here before mathematicians did.

cards.title: Six neighbours beats eight
cards.text: Strategy games use hex grids because every neighbour is the same distance away.
points: **On a square grid**, diagonal moves are longer than straight ones.
**On hexes**, all six are equal. Movement rules get simpler.
**Cyberpunk's UI** leans on hexagons for exactly the look of this.

question.text: Why do bees build hexagonal cells rather than square ones?
options: Hexagons hold the most space for the least wall material
Hexagons are easier for bees to see
question.explain: Squares tessellate perfectly well. Hexagons just do it with less wax for the same storage.

cards.title: Now the part where you cheat
cards.text: So far only three shapes work. But there's a trick. It turns any square into a shape that still tiles — and it looks nothing like a square.

cards.title: M.C. Escher
cards.text: A Dutch artist who saw tiled walls in a Spanish palace. He spent the next forty years turning tessellations into lizards, birds and fish.
points: **He wasn't a mathematician.** He worked it out by drawing.
**Mathematicians later proved** he'd found rules they hadn't written down.
**Every one of his tiles** started as a triangle, square or hexagon.

cards.title: The tiles Escher saw in Spain
cards.alt: Interlocking tiled patterns on a wall of the Alhambra palace in Spain
cards.credit: gruban · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
cards.text: The Alhambra palace, covered in interlocking tile. He came home and spent forty years on it.

cards.title: Cut and slide
cards.text: Take a square. Cut a piece off one edge. Slide that exact piece to the opposite edge and tape it on.
points: **The area never changes.** You moved it, you didn't lose it.
**The edges still match** their neighbours perfectly.
**So it still tiles** — with no gaps, forever.

cards.title: Drag the slider and break the square
cards.text: The tiles stop being squares. They never stop fitting. That's the whole method.

cards.title: One tile, repeated
cards.alt: A geometric tessellation built from repeating shapes in three directions
cards.credit: Basile Morin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
cards.text: Every shape here started as a simple polygon that somebody cut and slid.

question.text: If you cut a piece off one edge of a square and slide it to the opposite edge, the new shape still tessellates.
question.explain: True. The edges still match up exactly, so the shapes still interlock. This is how Escher built every one of his tilings.

cards.title: Escher's method, demonstrated
cards.text: The Museum of Science shows the cut-and-slide done by hand on paper.

cards.title: You've used this without knowing
cards.text: Interlocking foam mats at the gym are cut-and-slide tiles. So is every jigsaw puzzle.
points: **The tab and the notch** are the same piece, moved.
**That's why they only fit one way** round.
**Game tilesets** use the same trick to hide the grid.

cards.title: Three things that shouldn't be true
cards.text: Regular shapes are the fussy ones. Once you drop the word 'regular', tessellation gets strange.

cards.title: Every single triangle works
cards.text: Not just equilateral ones. Draw the most lopsided triangle you can and it will still tile the plane.
points: **Two copies make a parallelogram.**
**Parallelograms tile easily** in rows.
**So every triangle does too.** No exceptions.

cards.title: Every quadrilateral works too
cards.text: Any four-sided shape at all. Even an ugly dented one. It tiles.
points: **Its four angles always total 360°.**
**Four copies meet at a point** and use up exactly one full turn.
**Meanwhile the neat regular pentagon** still can't.

question.text: A regular pentagon cannot tessellate, but any four-sided shape you draw can.
question.explain: True, and it's the best joke in geometry. A quadrilateral's angles always sum to 360°, which is exactly what a corner needs.

cards.text: Irregular pentagons CAN tile — but only 15 kinds exist. The 15th was found in 2015, and the proof that there are no more came in 2017.

cards.title: Shapes that fail alone can work together
cards.text: An octagon leaves 90° spare at each corner. A square is exactly 90°. Put them together and the gap disappears.

question.text: Put the steps of the angle test in order.
items: Check whether the answer is a whole number
question.explain: Sides, then angle, then divide, then check. If it isn't whole, the shape can't tile on its own.

terms.def: A covering of a flat surface with no gaps and no overlaps.
A shape with all sides equal and all angles equal.
The angle inside a shape at one corner.
A corner. In a tessellation, a point where tiles meet.
A tiling made from one regular polygon. Only three exist.
A tiling made from two or more regular polygons. There are eight.
A flat surface that goes on forever in every direction.
Sliding a shape without turning or flipping it.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **No gaps, no overlaps.** That's the whole definition.
**Only three regular shapes** tile alone: triangle, square, hexagon.
**Angles at a corner must total 360°.** Interior angle = (n − 2) × 180 ÷ n.
**Cut and slide** turns any square into a tile that still fits.

cards.title: Sliding, flipping, turning
cards.text: Week 2 is translation, reflection and rotation. You've already used translation — that's the slide in cut-and-slide.

options: A pattern of shapes with no gaps and no overlaps
A shape with all sides equal
A pattern made only from squares
quiz.explain: No gaps and no overlaps. The shapes don't have to be identical, and they don't have to be regular.
quiz.objective: Define a tessellation as a covering with no gaps and no overlaps

quiz.text: Which three regular polygons tessellate on their own?
quiz.explain: Only those three. Their interior angles — 60°, 90° and 120° — each divide into 360 exactly.
quiz.objective: Identify the three regular polygons that tessellate on their own

quiz.text: What must the angles around any vertex in a tessellation add up to? Digits only.
quiz.explain: 360° — one full turn. More than that and tiles overlap. Less and you get a gap.
quiz.objective: Calculate the interior angle of a regular polygon and test it against 360°

quiz.text: What is the interior angle of a regular octagon, in degrees? Digits only.
quiz.explain: (8 − 2) × 180 ÷ 8 = 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°. And 360 ÷ 135 = 2.67, so octagons can't tile alone.
quiz.objective: Calculate the interior angle of a regular polygon and test it against 360°

quiz.text: A regular pentagon has 108° corners. Why can't it tessellate?
options: Three make 324° and four make 432° — neither is 360°
It has an odd number of sides
quiz.explain: You can't fit a whole number of them around a point. Three leave a 36° gap; four would overlap.
quiz.objective: Explain why some regular polygons cannot tessellate

quiz.text: Any triangle, no matter how lopsided, will tessellate.
quiz.explain: True. Two copies of any triangle form a parallelogram, and parallelograms tile in rows.
quiz.objective: Explain why some regular polygons cannot tessellate

quiz.explain: False. Every triangle and every quadrilateral tessellates, regular or not. Meanwhile the perfectly regular pentagon cannot.
quiz.objective: Define a tessellation as a covering with no gaps and no overlaps

quiz.text: Put the angle test in order, from first step to last.
items: Check whether the answer is a whole number
quiz.explain: Sides, angle, divide, check. If the division isn't exact, the shape cannot tile on its own.
quiz.objective: Calculate the interior angle of a regular polygon and test it against 360°

quiz.text: You cut a piece off the left edge of a square and slide it onto the right edge. What happens?
quiz.explain: It still tiles. The edges still match their neighbours exactly — this is Escher's whole method.
quiz.objective: Create a tessellating tile using the cut-and-slide method

quiz.text: Why do octagons and squares tessellate together when octagons alone cannot?
options: The octagon leaves 90° spare, and a square is exactly 90°
Two octagons make 360° on their own
It only works if the squares are tilted
quiz.explain: Two octagons give 270°, leaving 90°. A square fills it exactly, so the corner reaches 360°.
quiz.objective: Identify the three regular polygons that tessellate on their own

quiz.text: Bees use hexagons because hexagons hold the most space for the least wall material.
quiz.explain: True. Squares tile just as well, but hexagons need less wax for the same storage.
quiz.objective: Identify the three regular polygons that tessellate on their own

quiz.text: How many regular polygons tessellate on their own? Digits only.
quiz.explain: Three: the equilateral triangle, the square and the regular hexagon. That's the complete list.
quiz.objective: Identify the three regular polygons that tessellate on their own

teacher.summary: Week 1 Maths covers tessellation of shapes, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. Delivered as a card deck with seven checkpoints and a 12-item quiz. The lesson is built around the vertex-angle argument — that angles at a corner must total 360° — rather than around pattern recognition, so it prepares directly for Week 2 (translation, reflection and rotation). Two interactive diagrams carry the load: one fans polygons around a point so the gap is visible, and one performs the cut-and-slide live.
discussion: Ask him to prove a decagon can't tessellate without being told the answer. If he reaches for (n − 2) × 180 ÷ n and then divides into 360, he has the method rather than a memorised list.
Ask why every quadrilateral tessellates but the regular pentagon doesn't. The answer — a quadrilateral's angles always total 360° — is the whole lesson in one sentence.
Ask him to find three tessellations in the room. Floor tiles, brickwork, fabric weave and window grilles all qualify.
Ask what changes if the surface is curved rather than flat. It's beyond the syllabus, but it's the question that leads to why a football needs pentagons.
teacher.extension: Have him make one cut-and-slide tile on squared paper, then repeat it eight times to show it tiles. Escher's entire method in fifteen minutes, and it produces something he can keep.
misconceptions: 'Tessellations have to use regular shapes.' Every triangle and every quadrilateral tessellates, however irregular. Regularity is neither necessary nor sufficient.
'Pentagons never tessellate.' Regular pentagons don't. Fifteen types of irregular convex pentagon do — the last was found in 2015.
'Any shape tiles if you rotate it enough.' The vertex angles must total exactly 360°. No amount of rearranging fixes a shape whose angle doesn't divide in.
'A shape with a gap is still a tessellation if the gap is small.' It isn't. The definition allows no gaps at all.
